Subject: Dedicated pool behavior under burst — observed tail latency spikes

Hi Aditya / Marissa,

Thanks again for the demo last week. We’re running a short pilot on the dedicated GPU pool this week and I want to surface an operational concern before our procurement kickoff next Monday.

What we observed: during a 45-minute ingest window yesterday our service hit the reserved GPU cap and started queuing. Average latency stayed in agreed thresholds (~150ms per token), but we saw repeated tail spikes (2–4s) for a subset of requests. That behavior popped up when we triggered a set of long-context reranks (2k tokens) concurrently with shorter generation traffic.

Ask: Gamma needs clarity on how Redwood defines throughput SLOs for reserved capacity and what fallback behaviors you will guarantee if bursts exceed the reserved pool (e.g., head-of-line blocking, partial throttling, or graceful degradation to a cheaper model). Procurement needs a written exception path we can include in the PO so our infra team isn’t surprised.

Can you share: a) the exact queueing policy for dedicated pools when concurrency > reserved units, b) whether you’ll provide a carve-out window for short bursts without impacting latency SLOs, and c) any commitment to crediting or compensating for repeated tail-latency incidents during pilot.

I’ve attached a CSV with the sample traces (throughput_test_results.csv) and highlighted the 3 incidents.

Appreciate a short reply with next steps — we’d like to finalize purchase language by COB Friday.

Best,

Thanks for the heads-up — I dug into the traces and ran a quick reproducibility test against a sandboxdedicated pool. Notes:

- Root cause: when reserved GPUs are saturated, new requests are placed into the per-pool request queue. Our default policy is FIFO with request bucketing by token-cost to avoid starvation (short requests are interleaved to maximize throughput). However, heavy long-context reranks can evict prefetched KV pages and trigger kernel preemption, which results in the tail spikes you saw.

- Short-term mitigation (what we can do for Gamma pilot within 48 hours):
  * Implement a temporary priority threshold: classify requests >1.5k tokens as "low-priority burst" and move them to a bounded overflow queue that only pulls X concurrent long-contexts (configurable, default X=2). This preserves short-request tail SLAs while allowing limited long-context throughput.
  * Activate an autoshed policy: if queue depth > Q_high, we will immediately route new short-generation traffic to a compatible smaller model variant (same family, quantized) in the same region to preserve short-tail latency.
  * Provide a one-off credit for any incident where short-request P95 > 500ms and we cannot apply the workaround within 2 hours.

- Long-term: we can recommend a dedicated burst slice (N GPUs) reserved only for long-context tasks — effectively a two-tier reserved pool — but that requires a capacity commit and will change the cost profile.

I’ve attached the test CSV and a short diagram of the proposed two-tier pool (dedicated_burst_arch_diagram.png).

If Aditya / Marissa want, I can draft the exact amendment language that defines the thresholds (Q_high, X, credit formula).
